Title: Treating Peripheral Artery Disease Naturally
Author: Michael Greger M.D. FACLM
Description: Check out one of my favorite case reports ever published.
Transcript:
Below is an approximation of this video’s audio content. To see any graphs, charts, graphics, images, and quotes to which Dr. Greger may be referring, watch the above video.
The first documented reversal of atherosclerosis in people was not in the coronary arteries going to the heart, but in the femoral arteries going to the legs. Globally, hundreds of millions suffer from peripheral artery disease, where atherosclerotic clogs impair blood flow to our extremities. This causes a cramping pain in the calves when walking called claudication. That was one of the reasons my grandmother was confined to a wheelchair, waiting to die—until her life was saved by evidence-based nutrition.
Thanks to Nathan Pritikin, her near-miraculous recovery from heart disease gave her 31 more years of vim and vigor on her own two feet. Her story is what inspired me to dedicate my life to this work—to go into medicine, to start NutritionFacts.org, to write How Not to Die, and, furthermore, to donate 100 percent of the proceeds from all my books (including this one) to charity. I just want to do for everyone’s family what Pritikin did for my family.
Approximately seven percent of individuals older than 60 may suffer from claudication. There are similar angioplasty and stent procedures for the arteries going to our legs, and similar randomized, controlled trials showing they offer no benefit compared to supervised exercise therapy and medical management. The IRONIC trial (Invasive Revascularization or Not in Intermittent Claudication), for example, found that such invasive procedures, including roto-rooter-type techniques, open surgery, and bypass operations, offered no long-term benefit. Ironic indeed. Such interventions, a 2025 review concluded, “can often lead to patient harm, including a ‘treatment trap’ in which an initial vascular procedure may lead to multiple additional procedures and even amputation.”
Is there anything we can do with diet? For the management of peripheral vascular disease, clinical practice guidelines recommend a “healthy diet rich in legumes, dietary fibre, nuts, fruits, and vegetables.” We’ve known for twenty-five years that even a partial replacement of animal protein with soy protein in our diet significantly improves artery function within weeks, but what about other beans? Enter “Daily Non-Soy Legume Consumption Reverses Vascular Impairment Due to Peripheral Artery Disease,” a study in which twenty-six patients were asked to consume half a cup of cooked beans, peas, lentils, or chickpeas each day for eight weeks. Two months of adding beans to their diet didn’t just slow down the progression of their disease. On average, the circulation in their legs got better.
Peripheral artery disease is typically diagnosed and monitored using the ankle-brachial index—the ratio of blood pressure at the ankle compared to the arm. If the index falls below 0.9, it indicates a clog in the flow of blood to the lower body. When study participants added some hummus or lentil soup to their diets, they experienced significant improvements in both their LDL cholesterol level and ankle-brachial index. In four of the participants, their ankle-brachial index even jumped into the normal range. The researchers concluded that “a legume-rich diet can elicit major improvements in arterial function.” The study didn’t have a control group, but peripheral artery disease patients tend to get worse, not better.
Resveratrol supplements, fish oil, and flaxseed all failed to improve claudication or walking performance. Other than legumes, are there other foods that may be particularly helpful for peripheral vascular disease?
A single pinch of plain garlic powder (just 300 milligrams) can significantly thin the blood four to six hours after consumption. Might this help patients with peripheral vascular disease? A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial out of Germany put it to the test.
Patients with peripheral vascular disease who couldn’t walk without pain for more than about a tenth of a mile were randomized to coated pills containing one-eighth of a teaspoon of garlic powder or placebo pills twice a day. The garlic benefit was relatively small, an increase of walking distance of about 29 percent compared to 18 percent on placebo, and took four to six weeks to manifest, but the amount of garlic powder used would cost less than a penny per day.
What if the entire diet were centered around healthy plant foods?
We have known since the 1950s, from one of the first-ever dietary cardiovascular disease reversal studies published, that, within days, we can effectively turn diseases like peripheral artery circulation on and off like a light switch––simply by switching people between an essentially fat-free plant-based diet, and the more conventional diet that contributed to the problem in the first place. The study was published in a top-tier journal, funded in part by the American Heart Association, yet it’s been largely memory-holed from existence.
The first randomized, controlled study pitting a plant-based diet versus the American Heart Association typical low-fat diet was presented in 1975 by Pritikin and colleagues. After five months of exercise on the American Heart diet, patients were able to walk three times farther. Great! But the same amount of exercise on a plant-based diet enabled patients with severe peripheral vascular disease to walk fifty times farther. Maximal walking time increased by 5,870 percent.
Pritikin researchers showed that claudication pain could be eliminated within 26 days in more than two thirds of patients. They started the study hardly able to walk much at all, but, on a healthy enough diet, could increase their walking from essentially zero to more than two hours a day in less than a month.
One of my favorite case reports was published by Pritikin in 1982. A forty-six-year-old physical education instructor couldn’t walk more than a hundred yards without extreme pain. No wonder, since both of the femoral arteries in his mid-thigh were 100 percent clogged up. Within twenty-six days at Pritikin’s live-in program, his cholesterol dropped by a hundred points, and he was able to walk miles with little pain. By the end of the year, he had walked 600 miles and jogged more than a thousand. The next year, he ran the Chicago Marathon. Jogging thousands of miles a year, his best time was five miles in forty-one minutes. “This average of 8:20 per mile is a remarkable achievement for a man who…was a candidate for a bilateral femoral artery bypass operation… had no pulses below the thigh four years earlier.”
The diet only works if you actually eat it, though. A group of Canadian researchers tried unsuccessfully to replicate Pritikin’s work by randomizing peripheral vascular disease patients to advice to eat either a Pritikin diet or an American Heart Association diet for a year, and they saw little difference in outcomes. You can guess why. Just because people are told to eat a specific diet doesn’t mean they actually do it.
Dr. David Katz, founding director of the Yale-Griffin Prevention Research Center and past president of the American College of Lifestyle Medicine, wrote an article entitled “Lifestyle Medicine and the Parable of the Tiny Parachute.” If there were a randomized, controlled experiment of parachutes that ended with a jumble of mangled bodies, quote-unquote “proving” that parachutes don’t work, you’d have to question what the intervention group actually did. Dr. Katz writes:
What if our parachutes were ridiculously tiny, each the size of a postage stamp? Or what if they were opened too late, each deployed within mere inches of the ground? Or maybe they were both too little and too late. In that case, our experiment actually tells us nothing about the value of parachutes. It simply tells us that too little is too little, and too late is too late.
Even contemporary trials that show plant-based diets reverse endothelial dysfunction in patients with peripheral arterial disease are limited in their generalization due to compliance issues. About one in five peripheral arterial disease patients were unwilling to participate in a trial in which they risked being randomized into a plant-based group, and, further, about one in five who did end up in the plant-based group dropped out before the four-month trial was complete. So, the significant improvement in their disease “may apply only to individuals capable of adhering to the intervention.”
